title: Old Wires, Big Problem: Why U.S. Flights Stopped on Friday
summary: On Friday afternoon, planes across the United States suddenly stopped taking off. Air traffic controllers ordered a ground stop for four hours from 3:54 p.m. Eastern time. It was the longest such stop since September 11, 2001. Workers for a company called L3Harris were replacing old copper telephone wires with new fibre-optic cables. Transport Secretary Sean Duffy said a router being worked on began flooding other systems with data, cutting off communication with planes. More than 15,000 flights were delayed or cancelled that day, affecting about 1.5 million passengers. On Saturday, more than 5,900 flights were cancelled and 7,000 delayed. The Federal Aviation Administration said flights should be back to normal by the end of Sunday. Duffy said it is still not known if the fault came from the wire work or the router. He warned it could happen again unless Congress pays to modernise air traffic control. President Donald Trump has asked for 30.1 billion dollars, and Duffy has said the system needs a 50 billion dollar overhaul.
why_it_matters: If your family is flying to visit relatives or for a holiday, a ground stop like this could delay or cancel your flight and change your trip plans.

keywords.explanation: A ground stop is when planes are told to stay on the ground and not take off.
Copper is a brownish metal used to make wires that carry signals.
A fibre-optic cable is a thin cable that sends signals as light.
A router is a device that sends data between computer systems.
To modernise something is to make it newer and better.
An overhaul is a big repair and rebuild of a whole system.

background_read: Air traffic controllers are the people who tell planes when it is safe to take off, fly, and land.
They talk to pilots using phones, radios, and computers, so if those links stop working, planes cannot safely move.
Old copper wires are being swapped for newer fibre-optic cables, which can carry signals faster and more reliably.
